entry.summary:

The Price of Greed

🔹A fox happened to fall into a well bucket and, as the rope turned, went down to the bottom of the well. Struggle as it might, it found no way out—until a hungry wolf came to the well's edge and lowered its head.

🔹The clever fox put on an act and cried out: "Down here a feast of food and comfort awaits, but I can't manage it alone; if you'd like to share the meal, get into the upper bucket so you can come down to me!"

🔹The greedy wolf leapt without a moment's hesitation and sat in the upper bucket. Since the wolf was heavier, its bucket hurtled downward, and at the same time the rope turned and drew the fox's bucket upward.

🔹Midway up the well, the two buckets passed each other. The wolf cried out in astonishment: "Where are you off to, friend?!"

🔹The fox laughed and said: "That's the way of this wheel of fortune—unless one goes down, the other never comes up!" The fox reached the bright mouth of the well and sprang out, while the wolf was left behind in the dark depths.

#حکایت@Farsna

While Iran Khodro speaks of 78% localization and Saipa of 81% localization, and the assemblers also have a share of less than 40%, the question arises as to why localization has not been able to protect prices against currency shocks.
🔸To curb this cycle and cut the car market's psychological and real dependence on the dollar, the policymaker has no choice but to open the doors to targeted imports at times when relative stability prevails in the management of the country's foreign exchange resources, so that part of the foreign currency is allocated to the entry of economy cars—a strategy that can break the monopoly and save the market from profiteering./ Fars

entry.summary:

Source: @FarsNA

Domestic car prices are peaking ahead of the dollar🔹Car prices in the market have become sticky to the currency—a trend that accelerates upward whenever the exchange rate climbs. Today, cars that were once considered economy models have crossed into the billions of tomans.🔹This dependence on the currency, especially over the past year, has opened a deep gap between people's purchasing power and real prices. Last autumn, around this same time, the market was at completely different price levels, but persistent currency instability released the spring of prices.🔹Market statistics from the past year lay bare the depth of this jump: the Dena Automatic, which was around 1 billion and 300 million tomans at this point last year, has now reached about 4 billion tomans, and in the assembled-products segment, Lamari has climbed from 2 billion and 500 million tomans last year to 7 billion and 400 million tomans.🔹The car market's dependence on dollar fluctuations stands in clear contradiction to the claim of self-sufficiency. While Iran Khodro cites 78 percent localization and Saipa 81 percent, and assemblers hold a share of less than 40 percent, the question arises: why has localization failed to shield prices from currency shocks?🔸To curb this cycle and sever the car market's psychological and real dependence on the dollar, policymakers have no choice but to open the doors to targeted imports at times when relative stability prevails in the country's management of currency resources, so that part of the currency is channeled into bringing in economy cars—a strategy that can break the monopoly and rescue the market from profiteering.@Farsna - Link

One of the important yet under-examined questions in Iran's contemporary history is why Iran, in the age of colonialism, despite its economic and military weakness and its proximity to two great imperial powers, managed to preserve its political independence and avoid becoming a formal colony. In the nineteenth century, before the discovery of oil, Iran—unlike India—did not possess vast, contiguous agricultural lands with a high capacity for producing commercial crops. Unlike China, it had no consumer market with a population in the hundreds of millions, and unlike certain other territories, known gold and silver mines were not the primary source of its economic appeal to colonial powers. Nor was Iran part of the Ottoman Empire, such that it would have been caught up in the partition of Ottoman territories among the European powers. Nevertheless, Iran held extraordinary geopolitical importance. Its geographic position—between Tsarist Russia and British-ruled India—had made the country one of the most important arenas of imperial rivalry. Under such circumstances, Iran's survival cannot be attributed merely to chance or to a lack of resources attractive to colonialists. entry.title: [FarsNA] New details on the wells that swallowed Parishan's share🔹The global…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @FarsNA

New details on the wells that swallowed Parishan's share🔹The global registration of Gahar Lake in Lorestan under the Ramsar Convention has once again drawn attention to the status of Iran's registered wetlands.🔹Some of these wetlands have been grappling with drought for years and are still deprived of their water rights and an effective plan to restore natural conditions.🔹Parishan Wetland in Fars Province, with nearly two decades of poor conditions and hundreds of water-extraction wells, and Gavkhouni Wetland in Isfahan Province, despite the allocation of water rights and water releases into the Zayandeh Rud, are two examples of this situation.🔹Parishan Wetland has been in poor condition for about 16 to 18 years. One of the main reasons for this is the wetland's particular hydrological characteristics.🔹Parishan is one of the few wetlands in the country that does not lie at the end of a permanent river's course and has no direct river inflow. Its main source of water is rainfall and the floods that occur in the region.🔹For this reason, Parishan is more fragile than wetlands fed by permanent rivers.🔹When the groundwater table was high, rainfall would saturate the soil and raise the wetland's water level.🔹In fact, the connection between rainfall, the aquifer, and the wetland was such that water could quickly accumulate in the region and create suitable conditions for the wetland.🔹But in recent years, with increased extraction from groundwater resources, this situation has changed. There are about 490 illegal wells in the Parishan area.🖼But what plan is in place to prevent these conditions from continuing?Read here@Farsna

In these questions, the Alberta government is not merely seeking to change executive policies but is calling for a constitutional amendment and a redefinition of the legal relationship between the federal government and the provinces. From February 28 to today, gasoline has gotten more expensive in 145 countries. 29 countries have seen serious street protests. Paris made 1,800 arrests in a single day, Bolivia saw 17 killed, and in Tirana government buildings went up in flames.

So the short answer is: yes, the shock of this war reached the entire world.

But the chart says something else too — something more important.

Point one: Nigeria had a 75 percent fuel price hike and stayed calm. Albania had 17 percent and went up in flames.

▪️Stating that unless it is determined how much responsibility each party bears for derailing the agreement, and as long as leniency is shown in this regard, support campaigns will not achieve the desired outcome, he said: Supporting the agreement requires, beyond civil actions and popular campaigns, serious and responsible action by official authorities, especially the government.

▪️Ali Mehrabadi noted that despite the follow-ups, no permit has yet been issued for a gathering in support of the agreement, which the Reform Front of Iran had previously requested, and added: As long as marginal confrontations and the chanting of harsh slogans continue at nighttime gatherings, and no appropriate action is taken by official authorities — particularly the government — to manage these conditions, such campaigns in support of the agreement will yield little and will not be widely embraced by the public.

▪️In conclusion, the Head of the Reform Front of Hamadan Province, while commending the intentions of the organizers of these campaigns, expressed hope that these efforts will bear fruit, and emphasized: Alongside these actions, it is essential that Mr. Pezeshkian and the government take serious and effective measures to support those who find themselves in these difficult conditions.

🔹The Reform Front of Iran's address on social networks: Telegram, Instagram, X (Twitter)

Amir Mohammad Hatami, an 18-year-old from Shahin Shahr in Isfahan, was killed by a point-blank shot to his right eye after being wounded and taken into custody on the evening of 19 Dey. After 20 days of searching prisons, morgues, and security centers, his family finally identified his body—which bore signs of torture—by an old scar on his right shoulder. The 18-year-old was of Bakhtiari origin and lived in Shahin Shahr in Isfahan province. In the first days, Hatami's family had no information about their son's detention and did not know where he had been taken after being wounded. According to a source close to the family, during the search, Hatami's family would open about 100 black body bags every day in the hope of finding their son. Finally, after 20 days of searching, someone contacted the family and asked them to send a family member to identify a body. The source said: "When we went to identify Amir Mohammad, his body was inside a black bag. The blood on his body had dried and he was unrecognizable. His body and face were completely bruised." He added that Amir Mohammad's ears were severely damaged, his eyes had been gouged out, and numerous marks of injury were visible on his body. Amir Mohammad worked as a mechanic. According to those close to him, despite his young age, he was highly skilled in this trade and was known as "Osta" in Shahin Shahr. Those who knew Amir Mohammad described him as a hardworking, kind, and responsible young man who, in addition to helping provide for his family, also cared about supporting child laborers. iranintl 📡 @VahidOnline

But only to create instability.

I've been holding on to this video for several years now, to attach to a note in my journals about left and right (which I still haven't had the chance to finish).

Although the concepts of left and right are inadequate and vague for capturing the complexities of today's global political landscape, they can still be somewhat useful for conveying and understanding messages.

In this video, Bezmenov, a KGB associate and insider, explains that using leftists is useful—"but only up to the point of creating instability in countries."

The interview was recorded in 1984.

Link

Let me emphasize once again: if you ask my opinion, for our country today we want neither left nor right. What we want is a different way of looking at things—one that aligns with the left on some positions and with the right on others.

Almost the opposite of most of those segments that have today been adopted from—or have ended up aligning with—the conventional left and right in our political structure.

entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴Not every belief that keeps us alive is necessarily true. "Practical…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴Not every belief that keeps us alive is necessarily true. "Practical usefulness does not imply theoretical truth." ✍ Mostafa Malekian

🔹The fact that a belief helps us in practice, solves a problem, or even contributes to our survival does not by itself show that the belief corresponds to reality. Being useful is one thing; being true is another. You cannot infer the latter from the former.

A medicine may cure our headache, yet the theory on which the medicine was based may not be correct. The drug's effectiveness in curing does not by itself prove the correctness of the theory behind it.

The same distinction must be kept in mind in the discussion of evolution. If we accept Darwin's theory, we must note that the persistence of our beliefs, feelings, emotions, and desires does not necessarily mean they show us the truth; they may have persisted because they helped preserve the survival of our species.

That something ensures the survival of the human species is different from its expressing the truth. We may have held a belief, and that very belief kept our species alive; but from this one cannot conclude that the belief was certainly correct. It is even possible that awareness of a truth, rather than aiding our survival, endangers it.

🔹When people have said since ancient times that "the truth is bitter," one of its meanings is this: what is true is not always life-preserving for us or a guarantor of our continued existence.

🔹Therefore, even if a belief seems perfectly clear and self-evident to us and generation after generation has lived with it, this mere persistence and usefulness does not prove that it is true.

🔹From the fact that "this belief has helped our survival," one cannot conclude that "therefore this belief is true."

➖Part of the lecture "Critique_of_the_Book_Analytical_Idealism" @mostafamalekian

"Feeling the Sorrow of Others" in a Tale by Saadi

You've heard me say this a lot, but since I…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Strategy at the Individual Level

You've heard me say this a lot, but since I brought up resource constraints, I'd like to repeat it once more:

Whenever someone tells me, "Starting today, I want to do such-and-such" (study a language, read books, exercise, ...),

my first question to them is:

"What are you going to stop doing starting today?" Because your day wasn't 23.5 hours before, that you'd now want to add half an hour to it. Until yesterday you also had 24 hours, and now you want to add a quarter hour or half an hour of a new activity to it. So something has to give.

Now either you're going to watch fewer movies,
or go to fewer parties,
or sleep less,
or exercise less,
or check Instagram and Telegram less,
or ...

If someone hasn't clearly answered this second question, that first thing they said is just a passing fad. Sooner or later, you should expect them to rattle off all sorts of excuses for "it not working out" and "giving up."

Being Iranian is a blend of wisdom, justice, liberty, and love—four pillars on which our culture rests. A culture's pillars should not be judged merely by how faithfully people adhere to them today; we must also ask what values a culture possesses that enable it to recognize and correct its own shortcomings. These four pillars are not a claim that Iranians are flawless; they are an ethical and cultural horizon we can lean on to build a better society. Wisdom, justice, liberty, and love are neither imported values nor newly invented ideals; they are rooted in our own history and intellectual and cultural heritage. From the Avesta and the teachings of truth and asha, to the admonition books of ancient Iran and their emphasis on wisdom and justice; from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and its praise of wisdom, justice, and liberty, to the works of Saadi and other great figures of Persian literature who have honored love and humanism—the continuity of these values is visible. These four pillars are not meant to describe the behavior of all Iranians in all eras. They are criteria rooted in our culture, and we can even draw on them to critique the shortcomings of today's society. If there is foolishness, wisdom remains a virtue; if there is injustice, justice remains a value; if there is baseness and flattery, liberty remains an ideal; and if there is violence and hatred, love remains an ethical necessity.

entry.title:
[bamotamem] Strategy hurts (1)
Following my previous point about the vision, it's worth…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Strategy hurts (1)

Following my previous point about the vision, it's worth adding a few more notes. I've said these things many times over the years. But repeating them is useful too. They're worth constantly repeating and hearing.

My friends.

Strategy is always and always accompanied by resource allocation. The resources at our disposal (money, time, connections, etc.) are limited, and strategy is supposed to help us allocate these limited resources better.

"Resource allocation" is different from "resource distribution."

Resource distribution means I spread whatever I have across different tasks, different resources, different departments, and try to make sure everyone gets a piece.

Resource allocation is a scientific and precise term with a specific meaning.

Resource allocation means we think about who we want to give these limited resources to (and who we don't).

By defining, formulating, and executing strategy, we always create dissatisfied people. If you see that a strategy meeting was held, everyone sat together and talked, and at the end everyone came out smiling, know that the only thing wasted in there was the sugar and tea and the fruit of the meeting.

Must, must, must, some people come out of the strategy meeting upset. These are the same managers, the same departments, and the same projects that have been allocated fewer resources.

#استراتژی

"Feeling the Sorrow of Others" in a Tale by Saadi

In his tale of the Damascus famine, Saadi speaks of a man who is not himself in straitened circumstances, yet the suffering of the hungry robs him of pleasure. Can one, in a time of war, economic hardship, and insecurity, be concerned about the suffering of others and still carry on with life?

In this episode, inspired by Saadi's tale, we turn to the meaning of empathy in difficult days; we speak about the necessity of compassion and of lessening the suffering of others, and we reflect on how the flood of images of suffering on social media can gradually numb us. entry.title: [mostafamalekian] 🔴Can one be a materialist without denying God? | The difference between…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴Can one be a materialist without denying God? | The difference between materialism and moral materialism ✍ Mostafa Malekian

Materialism comes in two very distinct forms: one is "philosophical materialism" and the other is "moral materialism" or "value materialism." To clarify the difference, we need to see what each one claims.

Who is a materialist in the philosophical sense?

Philosophical materialism is a view of the universe. Those who hold this view believe that nothing exists in the world unless it is the product of the exchange of matter and energy—that is, the product of matter converting into energy or energy converting into matter.

🔹But what about our mind and our mental states? Materialists hold two positions here: Some say that mind and mental states do not exist at all. If we ask why we believe they exist, they answer that this belief is a product of our "folk psychology"; it is within this psychology that something called mind and mental states appears to exist.

🔹Others say that mind and mental states do exist, but they are reducible to the same exchange of matter and energy. In a sense, mind and mental phenomena too seem to be wearing a disguise; otherwise, they too are simply material phenomena.

🔹With such a view, one can no longer believe in the existence of God or a non-material spirit and soul. This is philosophical materialism—a view that many philosophers have held throughout history.

But what is moral materialism?

Moral materialism has nothing to do with philosophical materialism at all; rather, it is a theory in axiology whose gist is this: the only thing that matters in life is wealth.

Here I use "wealth" in a sense that also includes money, property, and assets.

If you believe that in human life only one thing has value, and that is wealth, you are a moral materialist. Since value means having importance, it can be put more simply: in this view, only wealth is important and nothing else in life matters.

According to this view, wealth—for having a good and ideal life—is both a "necessary condition" and a "sufficient condition":

• Necessary condition means that unless you are wealthy, you will not have a good life.

• Sufficient condition means that if you have wealth, you no longer need anything else for a good life.

Most of us human beings, in most historical periods, have not been materialists in the first sense; but the majority of us are materialists in the second sense.

➖From the lecture "Balance and Equilibrium between Money and Spirituality"
@mostafamalekian

Across the Iranian plateau, thousands of ancient and historical sites are scattered, each one a part of the history and civilization of this land. At some of these sites, different historical layers have formed on top of one another, becoming the earliest cores around which today's metropolises took shape. Ahvaz is one such metropolis — a city whose historical and civilizational record stretches back centuries before Islam. Despite this significance, the city's ancient heritage has been at risk of destruction over the past two decades because of metro excavations.

The project, which had been suspended since 1394 owing to financial problems and disputes between the municipality and the contractor, is now set to restart with a new contractor along the same route as before. Yet archaeologists had repeatedly warned that this area is likely linked to the ancient cities of Taryana and Hormoz Ardashir, and the artifacts discovered during metro excavation in these areas only strengthen that likelihood. But as the evidence suggests, city officials intend to resume the project without taking these warnings into account.

The story of the martyrdom of a member of the Leader's special office, the martyr🔹 Martyr Mohammad Reza Saghafi-Far was one of the members of the special office of the martyred Leader of the Revolution. From 1368, upon joining the Corps of the Wali al-Amr, he served the martyred Leader of the Revolution with love and sincerity, and after retirement, by order of His Eminence, he remained by his side. On the ninth of Esfand 1404, though that day's shift was not his and he had gone to the workplace in place of his colleague, he was martyred in an American-Zionist attack.🔹The martyr's family say that Martyr Saghafi-Far's devotion was not limited to physical security alone; he was also steeped in ideals. His wife shares a moving memory: "My husband served the family of the martyred Leader of the Revolution for thirty years as a bodyguard, with love and devotion. After he retired, His Eminence the Leader had told one of his sons to call him so that he could speak with him. Our martyred Leader had told my husband: 'Mr. Saghafi! Where do you want to go?' My husband had said: 'Dear Leader! I have retired; I only had this much worthiness to be with you until now.' His Eminence had said: 'You are my fellow townsman and you are a Khorasani. Where do you want to go? From now on, come and be my assistant.' Upon hearing these words of our martyred Leader, my husband became very happy and would tell his daughter, 'I must remain by the Leader's side until the reappearance of Imam Zaman (may God Almighty hasten his blessed relief),' and he kept this pledge until his last breath."🔹His wife says, "We wished to meet with the Leader, but he would not get us a meeting card and would say, go and stand in line like ordinary people."🔹On the ninth of Esfand, the day of the incident, it was as if the lot of martyrdom had fallen to his name. His colleagues say that day was not his shift, but he stepped into the field in place of his colleague. His wife has a strange account of the morning of that day: "He did not take his bag of documents, his watch, or his ring with him; it was as if he knew he would not need these on this shift." He went with a light spirit, carrying none of his worldly attachments with him.@Farsna

"Feeling the Sorrow of Others" in a Tale by Saadi

In his tale of the Damascus famine, Saadi speaks of a man who is not himself in straitened circumstances, yet the suffering of the hungry robs him of pleasure. Can one, in a time of war, economic hardship, and insecurity, both worry about the suffering of others and continue living?

Did Vance really say that? Persian-language media inside and outside Iran have reported that JD Vance acknowledged his disagreement with Donald Trump over the Iran issue. It's a strange and unprecedented piece of news, and it doesn't square with diplomatic etiquette in America. Vance may indeed disagree with Trump over war or Iran, but airing it before the media is unusual in every respect. So it seems to me that the media made an error in the initial drafting of this news. The Persian text of the report also doesn't indicate that Vance was referring to his disagreement with Trump. In my view, the pronoun in his sentence refers to Tucker Carlson, not to Trump. These days my internet access is limited and I can't verify this news, so the outlets that published it should look into it further. False and imprecise news, even in the field of foreign affairs, doesn't seem all that dangerous, but it is in fact very dangerous, because relying on such news leads to analyses of the kind Saeed Laylaz produces! entry.title:
[bamotamem] "A collection of all good things" is not a strategy
Yesterday I watched the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

"A collection of all good things" is not a strategy

Yesterday I watched the conversation between Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi and Mr. Mohammad Fazeli.

I hold both of these dear gentlemen in respect, and the points Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi made about macroeconomics were certainly instructive for me and all his students (as they always have been).

But at one point in the conversation, Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi said about the 20-year Vision Document: "We drafted this document in 1384, when Ahmadinejad had not yet come to power, and the document's goals seemed achievable."

Linking the failure to realize the Vision Document to Ahmadinejad's coming to power (which certainly dealt a great blow to national interests) does not seem logical to me.

The Vision Document was a completely wrong document from the very beginning. It was a beautifully written essay that had no strategic nature (while an upstream document of this kind should naturally have a strategic nature).

This document was "a collection of all good and attractive things." Strategy is not of this kind. Strategy means letting go of many good things and setting priorities among other good things, and specifying which good thing we are willing to sacrifice for the sake of another good thing.

If these questions are not answered in a document, that document is nothing more than an essay.

I consider it one of my honors that from those very years, when I was teaching strategy, I taught this document as an example of a completely wrong document, and I told my students that this document is not a vision—it is merely eye-catching.

That document was wrong on the first day too; with Ahmadinejad or without Ahmadinejad, for Iran or for Saudi Arabia or for America.

It was a beautiful essay that seemed poetic and attractive. But my judgment is that anyone with even a little literacy in strategy would never have been willing to sign beneath that essay.

#Maybe_Temporary

Negotiation as a tactic of war or a tool in the service of peace? Mohammad-Baqer Qalibaf, the Speaker of the Parliament, has repeated for the umpteenth time that "we fight and we negotiate." Yes. There is no contradiction between war and negotiation such that one must choose one or the other. But what is meant by negotiation? Is negotiation a tool for achieving peace and ending hostility? Or is it a tactic to create opportunities and buy time to equip oneself in order to be better prepared to continue the war? If the second meaning is intended, then framing the war-negotiation duality is pointless, because in that case negotiation amounts to nothing more than a tactic of war. But if what is meant by negotiation is ending the war and achieving peace, then the war-peace duality is a more logical substitute for the war-negotiation duality. War and peace, however, unlike war and negotiation, are contradictory and cannot be reconciled; therefore, one must inevitably choose between them. In my view, our country has now reached a point where it must inevitably choose between war and peace. Mr. Qalibaf, as the head of Iran's negotiating team, is obliged to confront public opinion on this matter with greater candor and courage. It is the responsibility of Mr. Qalibaf and other officials who speak on this matter to give these terms conceptual clarity. Words and expressions without conceptual clarity are like balloons full of air and serve more for entertainment than for conveying a message and clarifying a goal! The political atmosphere of our country has become so bloated from the sheer volume and accumulation of undefined words that everyone is bewildered and dazed! #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

Unprecedented drop in US commercial oil reserves over the past 8 months 🔹According to the latest data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the country's commercial crude oil reserves fell by 8.56 million barrels in the week ending October 9, reaching approximately 415.58 million barrels.🔹This weekly decline is the largest in the past eight months and points to a significant shift in the state of US oil inventories.🔹Over the same period, US strategic crude oil reserves remained unchanged at 282.9 million barrels. The recorded decline was therefore mainly in commercial reserves, with strategic reserve inventories unchanged.🔹The data also shows that diesel and other distillate fuel reserves fell by 2.53 million barrels to 102.61 million barrels.🔹The sharp drop in commercial crude oil reserves could, if sustained, support oil prices; however, a precise assessment of its impact on the market requires examining domestic oil production, imports and exports, refinery utilization rates, and fuel demand trends in the US simultaneously.🔹The rise in gasoline reserves also shows that changes in petroleum product inventories have not been uniform, and no definitive conclusion about the overall state of demand can be drawn solely from the decline in crude oil reserves.@Farsna - Link

⭕️ The need for greater caution among military and civilian officials to avoid assassination in the coming weeks

Despite certain warnings, it was wrongly assumed that America would not assassinate General Soleimani during his trip to Iraq. Unfortunately, it did. We lost our strongest strategic commander. Despite warning signs, it was wrongly assumed that Israel/America would not assassinate our top-tier military commanders in Tehran in the middle of negotiations. Sufficient caution was not taken, and unfortunately, on a single day and sometimes in a single above-ground location within firing range, a group of our most capable commanders were assassinated on the first day of the 12-day war, and we lost martyrs of the caliber of Major General Bagheri and Major General Rashid.

Despite numerous warning signs, it was wrongly assumed that Israel/America would not be so foolish and audacious as to assassinate the Commander-in-Chief and a source of emulation whose martyrdom injects unprecedented strength and blood into the homeland resistance. It committed exactly such folly and audacity, and we lost Iran's martyred leader on the first day of the Ramadan war.

Despite the high risk and bare-minimum protective measures, meetings of military and security commanders were held "above ground" all at once and became assassination targets, and on the first day of the Ramadan war we lost a large number of our most elite commanders and officials. It was obvious that national politicians of the caliber of Ali Larijani — who have the capacity to create leverage and open paths without abandoning the requirements of national power — were exposed to Israeli assassination. Even so, sufficient caution was again not taken, and he was placed "above ground" within firing range, and we lost the martyr Larijani.

From today until at least Dey 10 (the start of the new Democratic Congress), it is also clear that the risk of assassination by Israel or America is high, yet unfortunately, again and again and without sufficient caution, high-ranking civilian and military officials gather at funeral ceremonies at Masjid-e Noor, exhibitions, trips, and meetings — and even the meetings of the heads of the branches are held above ground.

Martyrdom in the path of Iran and the collective good of Iranians is an honor, and the courage of officials in high-risk conditions is commendable; but national responsibility and the damage that the assassination of any national figure in the current conditions inflicts on the country — learning from the above miscalculations and from the proven ability of the criminal Israel to carry out terrorist operations — demands that in the coming weeks, far more than today, protective precautions be observed regarding the location of meetings and high-risk, unnecessary programs. Respected officials! Dear commanders! Please, for the sake of Iran, in these weeks exercise far greater caution and care so that you are not assassinated by Israel or America. In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful

📌The auspicious birth of Hazrat Zainab Kubra (peace be upon her) — the epitome of patience and perseverance and the standard-bearer of loyalty in the most difficult arenas of divine trial — is a reminder of human glory that kept the lamp of hope alight amid suffering and affliction, and with faith and courage, etched an enduring epic of sacrifice and responsibility.

Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf

🔸October 16, 2026, marks…
entry.summary:

Source: @Kayhan_online

🔰Second Anniversary of Yahya Sinwar's Martyrdom

🔸October 16, 2026, marks the second anniversary of the martyrdom of Yahya Sinwar, known as "Abu Ibrahim," former head of the political bureau of the Hamas movement — a figure whose life was intertwined with captivity and the political and military developments of Gaza.

🔸Sinwar was born in 1962 in the Khan Younis camp, into a family displaced from the city of Al-Majdal. The experience of living in the camp and the aftermath of the Nakba formed the social context for the shaping of his political outlook. He studied Arabic language at the Islamic University of Gaza and expanded his political activity in the student environment — a path that was accompanied by repeated arrests at the hands of the occupation forces.

🔸His longest period of captivity began in 1988 and continued until his release in 2011. In prison, Sinwar became one of the organizational officials of Hamas prisoners, learned Hebrew, and followed developments in the society and politics of the Zionist regime. His release in the "Wafa al-Ahrar" agreement, which led to the release of 1,027 Palestinian prisoners in exchange for the Israeli soldier "Gilad Shalit," brought the issue of prisoners more prominently into his political life.

🔸In 2017, he assumed the leadership of Hamas in the Gaza Strip and was elected for another term in 2021. After the assassination of the martyr Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran, Hamas announced on August 6, 2024, the election of Sinwar as head of the movement's political bureau — an election in the midst of war that entrusted the responsibility of political leadership of the movement to the leadership based in Gaza.

🔸Sinwar was martyred on October 16, 2024, during a clash with the forces of the occupation army in Tel al-Sultan, Rafah. The army of the Zionist regime announced his martyrdom the following day, and Hamas confirmed his martyrdom on October 18. According to published reports, the forces involved were initially unaware of his identity, and identification was carried out after the clash.

🔸Images of the final moments of the martyr Sinwar in a destroyed building in Tel al-Sultan became one of the most enduring scenes of the Gaza war — images that showed him wounded and throwing a piece of wood toward an Israeli drone.

🔘 Yes | Eitaa | Soroush+ | Instagram | Telegram

Death of Dr. Pirouz Mojtahedzadeh; Professor and Researcher of Political Geography and Geopolitics of Iran

Dr. Pirouz Mojtahedzadeh, professor and researcher of political geography and geopolitics of Iran, passed away in the early hours of today in London.

Dr. Pirouz Mojtahedzadeh, a political geographer and renowned Iranian researcher, was one of the figures who devoted an important part of his scholarly and research work to Iran's political geography, border issues, the Persian Gulf, and Iran's geopolitical position in the region. His name is linked to discussions concerning Iran's territorial integrity, the three islands, and the strategic importance of the Persian Gulf.

Throughout his scholarly career, Mojtahedzadeh contributed to discussions on political geography and Iran's national interests through authoring books and publishing articles and specialized viewpoints — a field in which knowledge of history, geography, and power relations is of fundamental importance for understanding Iran's position in the region. He was among the researchers who spent their lives studying Iran's land, history, and political situation. May his memory be cherished, and may his loss be condoled to his family, friends, academic colleagues, and the scholarly community of Iran.

entry.summary:

Source: @javadimr

◀️ Daily Note⭕️ From "The Tenants" to "A House on the Verge of Collapse"; Iranian Society Through the Lens of Decline🔻 Hadi Soleimani Qarah Gol, PhD in Sociology, Kharazmi University🔍The note "From The Tenants to A House on the Verge of Collapse" by Hadi Soleimani Qarah Gol, by comparing two cinematic images of "home," critiques narratives that view Iranian society primarily through the lens of crisis, loss, and decline.📚The author, referring to Mohsen Qaraei's film "The Caretaker," with the international title Falling House, and Dariush Mehrjui's film "The Tenants," shows that the home in Iranian cinema has repeatedly become a metaphor for narrating the collective condition; from a house caught in strife and decay to a house on the verge of demolition. These two films do not carry the same meaning, but both provide the possibility of speaking about society through the condition of the house.In continuation, the note considers this metaphor part of a long-standing pattern in thinking about Iran; a pattern that narrates society through the lens of backwardness, disorder, rupture, and collapse. The author emphasizes that real crises such as migration, distrust, poverty, generational conflict, and weak institutions do not in themselves mean the collapse of society, and "many problems" should not be equated with "decline."💬Against this narrative, the author speaks of "defending society"; a defense that means neither denying crises nor defending the status quo, but rather an effort to see society beyond its list of afflictions. Society, at the heart of crises, can still build new bonds, come to each other's aid, create new ways of living, protest or show solidarity, and form new orders from below.🔗Read the rest of this note on the website of the Iranian Sociological Association.#Iranian_Sociological_Association@iran_sociology

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] The murmurings of 14. Sohrab in the notebook "The Traveler" and "The Green…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

The murmurings of 14. Sohrab in the notebook "The Traveler" and "The Green Volume" was murmuring to himself: "The lover is always alone/ and the lover's hand is in the trembling hand of seconds/...He and the seconds sleep on light/ and he and the seconds give the best book in the world/ to the water/ and they know well/ that no fish ever/ untied the thousand and one knots of the river/ and at midnights with the old boat of illumination/ they set out on the waters of guidance/ and drive on until the manifestation of wonder." And: "Someone came and took my books/ drew a ceiling of the harmony of flowers over my head/ made my evening vast with repeated windows/ placed my table under the spirituality of rain." The contemplative Shirazi mystic also whispered to himself: "Seize the moment and drink in the rose garden, for the rose will not be there another week. Tear up the pages if you are my fellow student, for the knowledge of love is not in the notebook." And: "Speak of the minstrel and wine and seek less the secret of time, for no one has unraveled and no one will unravel this riddle through philosophy." And: "What is this tall ceiling, simple yet of many patterns? Of this riddle, no sage in the world is aware." What a strange creature the human being is! A two-legged migratory bird who passes night and day in this existence, estranged, in toil and turmoil. On one hand, he knows that acquiring knowledge and understanding is, in Aristotle's words, among the "virtues" that constitute the essence of your and my humanity; a knowledge found in books and notebooks that draws the wise in its wake. On the other hand, he sees wayfarers like Hafez and Sepehri, who were learned and erudite, at a stage of their existential journey laying down their shields, acknowledging the enigmatic and mysterious nature of existence, relinquishing the untying of knots, washing away the pages of lessons and exercises and notebooks and books and entrusting them to flowing water, placing "the burden of knowledge from the shoulders of the swallow onto the ground"; and they have tasted and savored a "transparent fear," a "wise silence," and a strange wonder and bewilderment that consumes the palate.

Quoted from the book: "Velvety Murmurings," Volume Two.
Author: Soroush Dabbagh

entry.title: [jalaeipour] The next war doesn't necessarily begin with the firing of the first missile.…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

The next war doesn't necessarily begin with the firing of the first missile. Before that, a battle is already underway — over truth, over assigning blame, over legitimizing military action. Who broke the agreement? Who started the conflict? Who will bear responsibility for the consequences of the next war? The answers to these questions may be constructed and locked in on the media battlefield before the military conflict even begins.

Take the narrative that has taken shape in recent days around attacks on oil tankers and commercial ships: that Iran deliberately violated the Islamabad Understanding and is therefore responsible for the collapse of the agreement and the possible escalation of war. That the attacks occurred is one thing; turning that into a definitive narrative of Iran's unilateral responsibility — without examining the obligations of the parties, the US naval blockade, and the sequence of military actions — is another. Sometimes, to build a misleading narrative, there's no need to fabricate reality at all; it's enough to select part of the truth and omit the rest.

We have seen this before, too, in attempts to discredit real images of the bombing of Tehran. Some media accounts claimed the images of destruction were staged and that the women seen in the photos were actresses who kept reappearing. An independent review of the images from Sabounchi Street in Tehran refuted that claim. Here, the issue wasn't merely the publication of a false news item; it was an attempt to make the audience doubt reality itself, even when confronted with documented images of destruction and war victims.

In the possible next stage of the war, we must be more vigilant than ever against three phenomena: Misinformation — false information spread unknowingly; Disinformation — fake and distorted information deliberately produced to deceive; and Malinformation — real information used to cause harm, for example by revealing the identity or location of individuals at risk. These three can be deployed simultaneously to sow panic, destroy public trust, deny the realities of war, and prepare public opinion to accept a new conflict.

In such conditions, the war propaganda headquarters, if it exists, must monitor the information space moment by moment and respond with speed, accuracy, and verifiable evidence. Of course, countering information warfare doesn't mean constructing counter-narratives or denying unpleasant realities. The main capital in this battle is public trust, and that capital is preserved only through honesty and transparency.

The war of narratives may, before the military war, produce one crucial outcome: whom the public considers the initiator of the war, whom it recognizes as the victim, and whom it holds responsible for the destruction that follows.

📢 Twelve water and electricity projects inaugurated in East Azerbaijan with a budget of 124,500 billion tomans

◀️ In the presence of Mohammad Jafar Qaempanah, Executive Deputy to the President, during a visit to East Azerbaijan province today, 23 Mehr, 12 projects — including 2 water and wastewater projects and 10 electricity infrastructure projects — with a total announced budget of 124,500 billion tomans were inaugurated.

◀️ Among the inaugurated projects are a water supply project serving 150 villages in the province with a budget of 665 billion tomans, and the Azarshahr wastewater treatment plant with its transmission and collection network, Module One, with a budget of 1,740 billion tomans, both implemented by the East Azerbaijan Water and Wastewater Company.

◀️ The water supply project for 150 villages includes drilling and equipping 25 wells, building 19 reservoirs, laying 165 kilometers of transmission lines and 137 kilometers of water distribution network, rehabilitating 12 kilometers of transmission line, and constructing 6 pumping stations. With this project coming online, a stable water supply will be provided for 150 villages comprising 10,427 households and a population of over 36,745.

◀️ The Azarshahr wastewater treatment plant, using the advanced SBR method with a daily treatment capacity of 8,100 cubic meters, will serve a population of over 84,000.

◀️ Additionally, 10 electricity infrastructure projects under the responsibility of the East Azerbaijan Regional Electricity Company have been inaugurated. These projects include a 230-kilovolt double-circuit cable line to supply the central GIS substation of Tabriz via the energy tunnel, the 230-kilovolt section of the central GIS substation of Tabriz, and eight line and substation projects.

◀️ The total expenditure for the electricity projects is announced at 11,095 billion tomans, and their implementation has created jobs for 400 people. The goals of these projects include increasing the reliability of electricity supply to central Tabriz and its subordinate counties, and meeting the electricity needs of industrial parks.

entry.title: [VahidOnline] Varisha Moradi's lawyers announced on Wednesday, 22 Mehr, that Branch 15 of the…

Source: @VahidOnline

Varisha Moradi's lawyers announced on Wednesday, 22 Mehr, that Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court — which had previously sentenced this political prisoner held in Evin to execution on charges of "membership in a rebel group" — insisted on its previous death sentence despite the Supreme Court's request to examine "deficiencies in the investigation."

Amir Sajjadi and Keyvan Azizi, Varisha Moradi's lawyers, speaking to "Emtedad," confirmed this news and stated that on Wednesday, 22 Mehr, they visited Branch 15 of the Revolutionary Court and received the verdict issued by this branch, and according to the notified verdict, they have 20 days to appeal to the Supreme Court.

According to them, this verdict was issued in a situation where the previous verdict of Branch 15 sentencing Varisha Moradi to death had been overturned by the reviewing branch in the Supreme Court after serious doubts were raised about the investigation; yet the aforementioned branch, without conducting the investigation requested by the Supreme Court, merely changed the title of the charge and once again sentenced Ms. Moradi to execution on the charge of membership in a rebel group.

Amir Sajjadi, stating that "in the lawyers' view, there are no sufficient and solid grounds for attributing such a charge to Varisha Moradi," emphasized: "Ms. Moradi has absolutely not been involved in any operations against the Islamic Republic, and her activities were solely related to her fight against ISIS in northern Syria."

Keyvan Azizi also, emphasizing that Varisha Moradi's lawyers will appeal within the legal deadline, expressed hope that "the Supreme Court, as in the previous instance, will give sufficient attention to the defenses and objections."

Varisha Moradi, who is currently imprisoned in Evin Prison, was arrested on 10 Mordad 1402 on the outskirts of Sanandaj, and on 5 Dey of the same year, upon completion of the interrogation stages, was transferred from the Ministry of Intelligence detention center known as Ward 209 of Evin Prison to the women's ward of this prison.

She was sentenced to execution on 20 Aban 1403 by Branch 15 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court on charges of "baghy" (armed uprising against the government). In an open letter from prison, she revealed that during her detention she was subjected to physical and psychological torture, death threats, and gender-based violence.

@VahidHeadline📡 @VahidOnline

entry.title: [darvishnameh] 💧 Environmental water rights: from allocation on paper to water reaching the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

💧 Environmental water rights: from allocation on paper to water reaching the wetland

The report "Regulatory Oversight of Environmental Water Rights Allocation under Table (7) of Article (37) of the Seventh Development Plan Law," prepared by Mehdi Rajabi and Ali Haji-Moradi in Shahrivar 1405, examines the gap between legal commitments and the actual delivery of water needed by ecosystems.

The report's findings for the water year 1403–1404 show that drought is not the only reason water rights are not being fulfilled; weaknesses in the allocation system, withdrawals along the route, lack of coordination among agencies, and the absence of transparent monitoring also play a role.

The report's central message is clear: releasing water from a dam alone does not mean environmental water rights have been secured. The evaluation criterion must be whether water reaches the target ecosystem, in a volume, quality, and timing suited to its needs.

The report emphasizes reforming water allocation under water-scarce conditions, online monitoring and public disclosure of data, controlling withdrawals along the route, and integrated management of river basins.

🌱 Environmental water rights must hold a stable place in water allocation decisions — a share whose provision does not depend on water left over after other uses.

entry.title:
[bamotamem] Large World Models (LWMs)
This conversation I had with ChatGPT isn't an ideal…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

Large World Models (LWMs)

This conversation I had with ChatGPT isn't an ideal example — it's even a bit misleading.

But it can, to some extent, illustrate the difference between a language model and a world model.

The current wave of AI will presumably die down once the current bubble bursts (and of course its amazing achievements and capabilities will stay with us).

In the next wave, we'll be dealing with large models of the world — LWMs, or Large World Models — that have a better grasp of what's possible and impossible in the physical world.

Of course, even now, the models Tesla uses in the automotive industry and Palantir uses in warfare are of the World Model variety. But even so — whether in terms of the technology and system architecture, or in terms of commercial and widespread access — we're still a very long way from "artificial intelligence capable of understanding the physical world."

This gap — contrary to all the hype — isn't just a matter of scale.

The maritime security company Vanguard also announced that four ships were targeted in these attacks. Failure of the National Suicide Prevention Program

Hamid Peyravi, secretary of the Suicide Prevention Taskforce of Tehran Province, acknowledging the rising suicide rates in Iran, noted: One reason for the increase in statistics since the 1380s could be the systematization of case recording. In other words, before the 80s, cases were not recorded properly, and once accurate and precise recording was put on the agenda, naturally the statistics go up.

He referred to the issuance of the National Suicide Prevention Program in Shahrivar of 1401 and said: The plan was that in the final year of the program — that is, this year — we would achieve a 10 percent reduction in suicide attempts and deaths caused by it, but unfortunately we did not reach the program's goals at all; there has even been an increase, especially in attempts.

The vice president of the Scientific Society for Suicide Prevention in Iran called suicide bereavement one of the worst and most complicated types of grief and said: Individuals blame themselves, feel guilt, engage in self-rumination, or are subjected to society's judgment and are rejected.

He continued: More than 7,000 deaths and more than 150,000 suicide attempts in a single year have affected a large number of Iranian families, but has anyone reached out to these families? How do they cope with this suffering, and do they seek help?

Peyravi said: Each suicide involves and affects 135 people, and therefore the scope of our work goes beyond the numbers that are announced.

Mr. Miliband, you say you have discussed ending "Iran's aggression" with Marco Rubio. By what legal, moral, or humanitarian standard do you consider Iran the aggressor?

Two nuclear powers attacked Iran twice — in the middle of negotiations — and in the course of those attacks committed horrific war crimes:

- Bombing an elementary school in Minab during class hours, killing dozens of children;

- Attacking a sports hall in Lamerd during a girls' volleyball team practice;

- Firing on the Iranian vessel Dena in international waters as it returned from a naval parade hosted by India, killing around 100 unarmed sailors;

- Assassinating political leaders and scientists;

- Bombing civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, universities, bridges, petrochemical complexes, fuel depots, pharmaceutical factories, and desalination facilities;

- Bombing nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards.

The US president openly threatened to destroy a civilization so that it would "never rise again," at a time when the option of a diplomatic solution was within reach.

And you call these actions "Iran's aggression"?

Under General Assembly Resolution 3314, the party that initiates the use of force in violation of the UN Charter is considered the aggressor. Iran did not initiate the attack. You know this; your European counterparts know it too.

You had told your party that Britain's entry into the Iraq war was a mistake. That war, too, was justified by the false claim that weapons existed which did not exist at all. You more than anyone else should recognize this familiar scenario.

I challenge you to explain how a nation defending itself against two nuclear powers that threaten to destroy its civilization can be labeled an aggressor.

Did you also speak with Rubio about ending the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran? Or do you lack sufficient independence of judgment to raise such a question?

One day I will reach my beloved. My country's flag dances with joy in the sky. My people are proud of being Iranian. The sound of the adhan comes from the mosque and all become devoted, and from the God of their own selves, the Creator of their sufferings, they are freed and dissolve into the absolute good of existence... Perhaps here, perhaps elsewhere... A note for the professor...

The exact side where Hitler was sitting in the front seat, next to his driver. The truck pushed the car to the other side of the intersection and came to a stop just before it could run over the car and crush it along with everyone inside. "We and Gazprom": A Documentary Account of Why Iran's Gas Industry Fell Behind

The second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast, titled "We and Gazprom," was screened today at the Atana Hotel in Tehran, attended by members of the Energy Commission of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, former and current energy officials, experts, and journalists. The documentary reviews Russia's experience in developing its gas industry to examine the obstacles facing the development of this industry in Iran and the role of Tehran-Moscow gas relations.

Focusing on the history of Russia's oil and gas industry, particularly the formation and expansion of the country's gas distribution network, the documentary seeks to examine the development paths of the gas industry in both Iran and Russia through the lens of historical experiences and strategic decisions.

In this episode, through conversations with veterans and experts of the gas industry, the question is raised: why has Iran, despite holding the world's second-largest natural gas reserves, been unable to develop its gas industry in proportion to its resource capacity and secure a more influential position in regional and global markets?

One of the documentary's central themes is the relationship between the abundance of gas resources, domestic pricing policy, and the development of gas industry infrastructure. Has the supply of cheap gas to consumers contributed to the sustainable development of this industry, or have pricing policies and rising domestic consumption constrained the resources needed for infrastructure investment and export development? The documentary seeks to examine various dimensions of this issue by presenting expert perspectives.

In another section, the documentary turns its attention to Iran-Russia gas relations—two countries that rank among the world's largest holders of natural gas reserves yet have taken different paths in developing gas exports. In this context, the question is raised: has Russia obstructed Iran's gas export development in recent years, and what impact has competition between the two countries had on Iran's export opportunities?

To watch the second episode of the "5 Khordad" podcast titled "We and Gazprom," follow the link below:
